record.paper_title: Major open problems in chaos theory and nonlinear dynamics
record.context_brief: Effective description of turbulence and chaos
record.original_question: Find an effective description of chaos and turbulence, especially turbulence arising under the Navier-Stokes flow, that is mathematically meaningful and practically useful rather than merely formal. Existing candidates mentioned in the source include Reynolds averaging, fractal dimension, SRB measures, horseshoes, and shadowing, but the source states that Reynolds averaging leads to an unsolvable closure problem for chaos and turbulence, fractal dimension lacks engineering value, SRB measures are elusive for most systems, and shadowing the entire turbulent attractor is still beyond current computational reach. The question is therefore what kind of averaging or other description can faithfully capture chaotic and turbulent dynamics in a way that is effective for engineering use.

evidence.quote: Here we mention a few major open problems: 1. an effective description of chaos and turbulence

More specifically, the mechanism of how chaotic dynamics operates is understood; how to effectively describe chaos in term of some sort of averaging is beyond reach (i.e. not tamed); it is not even clear what kind of averaging mean we should be after for! These questions will form the first major open problem to be discussed below.
A description of turbulence which is effective in engineering means a solution of the problem of turbulence.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ (for instance the periodic torus $\mathbb{T}^3$),
$$\partial_t u + (u \cdot \nabla) u = -\nabla p + \nu \Delta u + f, \qquad \nabla \cdot u = 0,$$
where $u : \Omega \times [0,\infty) \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is the velocity field, $p$ is the pressure, $\nu > 0$ is the kinematic viscosity, and $f$ is a (possibly stochastic or deterministic) forcing. For sufficiently high Reynolds number the resulting dynamics is widely observed to be turbulent and chaotic, and the long-time behaviour is governed by a complicated attracting set in an infinite-dimensional phase space.

Several mathematical frameworks have been proposed as effective descriptions of such chaotic/turbulent dynamics, including: (i) Reynolds averaging, in which one decomposes $u = \bar u + u'$ and derives evolution equations for the mean, leading to the (unclosed) Reynolds-stress closure problem; (ii) fractal/Hausdorff/box-counting dimension of the global attractor; (iii) Sinai–Ruelle–Bowen (SRB) measures, i.e. invariant measures whose conditional distributions on unstable manifolds are absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, used to describe statistical asymptotics of chaotic flows; (iv) Smale horseshoes embedded in the dynamics, providing symbolic-dynamics descriptions of chaos; and (v) shadowing, where true orbits remain close to numerically computed pseudo-orbits.

Problem. Produce a mathematically rigorous and quantitatively effective description of the chaotic/turbulent long-time dynamics of the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations that
(a) is well-defined for the full turbulent regime (high Reynolds number),
(b) yields closed, computable predictions for statistical observables (mean flow, correlations, energy spectra, transport coefficients, etc.) suitable for engineering use, and
(c) avoids the limitations of the existing candidates above: in particular, it should resolve or bypass the closure problem of Reynolds averaging, it should produce engineering-relevant quantities (unlike bare fractal dimension), it should not depend on the existence of an SRB measure that is not known to exist for generic Navier–Stokes flows, and it should not require shadowing the entire turbulent attractor at currently infeasible computational cost.

Equivalently: identify and rigorously justify a notion of "averaging" (or alternative effective description) of chaotic/turbulent Navier–Stokes dynamics whose outputs are both mathematically meaningful and practically useful.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of finding an effective, mathematically rigorous, and engineering-useful description of turbulence in the Navier–Stokes equations is widely regarded as one of the central unsolved problems of classical physics and mathematics; it remains open, with no known general closure theory, no proof of existence of SRB measures for 3D Navier–Stokes, and ongoing partial progress through approaches such as instanton/large-deviation methods, exact coherent structures, and data-driven closures.

status_evidence.title: Turbulence (Wikipedia)
status_evidence.snippet: Despite decades of research, there is no general theory of turbulence... the closure problem of Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations remains unsolved.
status_evidence.claim: No accepted effective description of turbulence exists; closure problem unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Clay Millennium Problem: Navier–Stokes
status_evidence.snippet: Understanding of the Navier–Stokes equations is considered to be a fundamental open problem.
status_evidence.claim: Foundational questions about Navier–Stokes dynamics remain open.
